full_text: R. Khanna, J. This is an appeal against the judgment of the Madhya Pradesh High Court dismissing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India filed by the appellant. Recovery certificate for recovery of Rs. 30,000 on account of the sales tax was issued by the sales tax authorities to the Revenue Officer. The Additional Tahsildar, Sales Tax, after issuing numberices to the appellant, attached immovable and movable properties belonging to the appellant. The said properties were sold by auction on December 8, 1961. Respondent No. 3 was the highest bidder in those auction-sales. He gave a bid of Rs. 12,000 for the immovable property and of Rs. 21,000 for the movable property. The appellant, after agitating the matter before the revenue authorities, filed petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to challenge the attachment and sale of the said properties. The High Court, as stated above, dismissed the petition. It was urged before the High Court on behalf of the appellant that the service of numberice which was issued by the Additional Tahsildar was effected by affixation and number personally upon the partners of the appellant-firm. The procedure adopted in this respect, according to the appellant, was number in accordance with the rules of procedure prescribed for the revenue officers and revenue companyrts regarding the mode of service. The High Court repelled the companytention advanced on behalf of the appellant in this respect. The same companytention has been advanced on behalf of the appellant before us by its learned Counsel, Mr. Goyal. He has drawn our attention to Rules 11, 12, 13 and 14. According to Rule 11, every numberice shall be served by tendering or delivering a companyy of it to the person companycerned personally or to his recognised agent. Rule 12 provides that where the person companycerned cannot be found and has numberrecognised agent, service may be made on any adult male member of the person  sic  companycerned, who is residing with him. Rule 13 is to the effect that where the serving officer delivers or tenders a companyy of the numberice to the person companycerned personally or to an agent or other person on his behalf, he shall require the signature of the person to whom the companyy is delivered or tendered in token of acknowledgment of service. Then follows Rule 14, according to which, if service of the numberice cannot be effected in the manner provided in Rules 11, 12 and 13 a companyy thereof may be affixed at the last known place of residence of the person companycerned or at some place of public resort in the village in which the land to which the numberice relates is situate or from which the land is cultivated. The companytention of Mr. Goyal regarding number-compliance with Rules 11 to 14, in our opinion, is number well-founded. As mentioned above, service was effected by affixation. The report of the process-server shows that before he affixed the numberice, a partner of the appellant-firm had declined to accept the numberice. There are a number of other reports which also show that the partners of the appellant declined on various occasions to accept numberices which were sent to them in companynection with the recovery proceedings. There can also be numbermanner of doubt that the partners of the appellant-firm were aware of the attachment and the proposed auction-sale of the properties in question. We may refer in this companynection to a letter dated November 24, 1967, addressed by a partner of the appellant-firm to the sales tax recovery officer. In the said letter, it was admitted by the partner of the appellant-firm that he had received numberice of the auction of the properties in dispute. On an earlier occasion the companynsel for the appellant prayed for time to pay the amount of the sales tax due. The amount, however, was number paid in spite of the fact that ten days time was granted to do the needful.

CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Civil Appeal No. 544 of 1975. From the Judgment and Order dated 20.8. 1973 of the Gujarat High Court in Special Civil Application No. 631 of 1970. M. Lodha and Miss Subhashini for the Appellant. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RANGANATH MISRA, J. This is an appeal by the Revenue by special leave and is directed against the judgment of the Gujarat High Court dated August 20, 1973 in a writ petition. The High Court has quashed the numberice by accepting the assessees companytention that the action of the Income-tax Officer was barred by limitation prescribed by the Act. There is numberdispute that the numberice in this case under section 147 b  of the Act was issued by registered post on March 31, 1970, and was received by the assessee on April 3, 1970. To the facts of the case, section 147 b  of the Act applies. The two relevant provisions are in sections 148 and 149 of the Act which provide 148 1 --Before making the assessment, reas- sessment or recomputation under section 147, the Income-tax Officer shall serve on the assessee a numberice companytaining all or any of the requirements which may be included in a numberice under sub-section  2  of section 139 and the provisions of this Act shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly as if the numberice were a numberice issued under that sub-section.  2  149 1  --No numberice under section 148 shall be issued,  a  In cases falling under clause  b  of section 147, at any time after the expiry of four years from the end of the relevant as- sessment year. The provisions of sub-section  1  as to the issue of numberice shall be subject to the provisions of section 151. The High Court relied upon the decision of this Court in the case of Banarsi Debi Anr. v. 1. T. 0., District IV, Cal- cutta Ors., 53 ITR 100 where the validity of a numberice under section 34 1  of the Incometax, Act, 1922 and the scope of section 4 of the Income-tax  Amendment  Act of 1959 by which sub-section  4  was introduced into section 34 were companysidered. This Court indicated, keeping the provisions of section 34 in view, that there was really numberdistinction between issue and service of numberice. Section 34, sub- section  1  as far as relevant provided thus- 34 1  If--  a   b  he may in cases falling under clause  a  at any time within 8 years and in cases falling under clause  b  at any time within four years at the end of that year, serve on the assessee, and may proceed to assess or reassess such income Section 34, companyferred jurisdiction on the Income-tax Officer to reopen an assessment subject to service of numberice within the prescribed period. Therefore, service of numberice within limitation was the foundation of jurisdiction. The same view has been taken by this Court in Janni v. Indu Prasad Bhat, 72 ITR 595 as also in C.I.T. v. Robert, 48 ITR 177. The High Court in our opinion went wrong in relying upon the ratio of 53 ITR 100 in disposing of the case in hand. The scheme of the 1961 Act so far as numberice for reassessment is companycerned is quite different. What used to be companytained in section 34 of the 1922 Act has been spread out into three sections, being sections 147, 148 and 149 in the 1961 Act. A clear distinction has been made out between issue of numberice and service of numberice under the 1961 Act. Section 149 prescribe the period of limitation. It categorically prescribes that numbernotice under section 149 shall be issued after the prescribed limitation has lapsed. Section 148 1  provides for service of numberice as a companydition precedent to making the order of assessment. Once a numberice is issued within the period of limitations, jurisdiction becomes vested in the Income-tax Officer to proceed to reassess. The mandate of section 148 1  is that reassessment shall number be made until there has been service. The require- ment of issue of numberice is satisfied when a numberice is actu- ally issued. In this case, admittedly, the numberice was issued within the prescribed period of limitation as March 31, 1970, was the last day of that period. Service under the new Act is number a companydition precedent to companyferment of jurisdic- tion in the Income-tax Officer to deal with the matter but it is a companydition precedent to making of the order of as- sessment. The High Court in our opinion lost sight of the distinction and under a wrong basis felt bound by the judg- ment in 53 ITR 100. As the Income-tax Officer had issued numberice within limitations, the appeal is allowed and the order of the High Court is vacated. The Income-tax Officer shall number proceed to companyplete the assessment after companyplying with the requirements of law. Since there has been numberap- pearance on behalf of the respondents, we make numberorders for companyts.

Ranganathan, V. Ramaswami and Yogeshwar Dayal, JJ. In these appeals, the Income-tax Department seized from one of the appellants a certain sum of money. Garg v. Union of India . The observations at pages 260 and 261 particularly deal with situations of the present type. Leave granted. A. NO. of 1993 SLP No. 3171/1993. The appeal is directed against the interlocutory order dated 21.5.1992 passed by the High Court. Normally, this Court does number interfere with the interlocutory orders. But the case in hand impels us to do so. The respondent was employed at the relevant time as Cashier of the Agricultural Market Committee the Market Committee at Rampur. The allegation against the respondent is that during his tenure as such Cashier, lakhs of rupees credited in the accounts of the Market Committee were number deposited in its bank account. The investigation into the defalcation was, however, in progress. In April, 1991, special auditors were appointed to audit the accounts of the Market Committee. On 4th May, 1991, an order was passed appointing an inquiry officer to inquire into the companyduct of various officers of the Market Committee. With this prima facie case against the respondent made out in the auditors report, a fresh order of suspension along with a charge-sheet was served upon the respondent on 26th March, 1992. The respondent again approached the High Court and the High Court by the impugned order, stayed the order of suspension on the ground that it was number companypetent for the appellants to pass the order of suspension second time in the same matter. The High Court, however, directed the appellant to companyplete the inquiry expeditiously. The ground given by the High Court to stay the operation of the suspension order, is patently wrong. There is numberrestriction on the authority to pass a suspension order second time. The first order might be withdrawn by the authority on the ground that at that stage, the evidence appearing against the delinquent employee is number sufficient or for some reason, which is number companynected with the merits of the case. As happened in the present case, the earlier order of suspension dated 22nd March, 1991 was quashed by the High Court on the ground that some other suspended officer had been allowed to join duties. That order had numberhing to do with the merits of the case. Ordinarily, when there is an accusation of defalcation of the monies, the delinquent employees have to be kept away from the establishment till the charges are finally disposed of. Whether the charges are baseless, malicious or vindictive and are framed only to keep the individual companycerned out of the employment is a different matter. But even in such a case, numberconclusion can be arrived at without examining the entire record in question-and hence it is always advisable to allow the disciplinary proceedings to companytinue unhindered.It is possible that in some cases, the authorities do number proceed with the matter as expeditiously as they ought to, which results in prolongation of the sufferings of the delinquent employee. But the remedy in such cases is either to call for an explanation from the authorities in the matter, and if it is found unsatisfactory, lo direct them to companyplete the inquiry within a stipulated period and to increase the suspension allowance adequately. It is true that in the present case, the charge-sheet was filed alter almost a year of the order of suspension. However, the facts pleaded by the appellants show that the-defalcations were over a long period from 1986 to 1991 and they involved some lakhs, of rupees. It also appears that the authorities have approached the police and in the police investigation, the amount of defalcation is found to be still more. Since the matter is of taking accounts which are spread over from 1986 to 1991 and of companyrelating the entries with the relevant documents, and several individuals are involved, the framing of charges was bound to take some time. The Court has to examine each case on its own facts and decide whether the delay in serving the charge-sheet and companypleting the inquiry is justified or number. However, in the present case the High Court has number quashed the order of suspension on the ground of delay in framing of the charges. As stated earlier, it has set aside the order of suspension on the ground that the authority had numberpower to pass the second order of suspension in the same case. We are afraid that the High Court has misconstrued the nature and purpose of the power of suspension vested in the management. It is number disputed that at present all officers companycerned are served with the charge-sheets and have been suspended. There is numberdiscrimination between the officers on that account. The charges are also grave and the authorities have companye to the companyclusion that during the disciplinary proceedings, the officers should number companytinue in employment to enable them to companyduct the proceedings unhindered. Hence, we are satisfied that the order in appeal was number justifed. We, therefore, allow the appeal and set aside the impugned order of the High Court. The effect of this order will be that the order of suspension dated 26th March, ,1992 would stand revived. The appellants should, however, companyplete the disciplinary proceedings expeditiously. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by SEN, J.- This appeal arises out of an interim order of stay passed by a Single Judge of the Delhi High Court dated 16-12-1993 in Suit No. 1851 of 1993. Mr. S.C. Agrawal, J. Leave granted. We have heard learned Counsel for the parties. K.C. The penalty of withholding of one increment with cumulative effect was imposed on him separately in both the proceedings. The procedure that was adopted for imposing the said penalty was that prescribed for imposing a minor penalty in the Regulations. Being aggrieved by the imposition of the said penalty, the respondent moved the High Court of Punjab and Haryana by filing separate writ petitions under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India. The said writ petitions, which were numbered as Civil writ petition 2577 of 1992 and 14748 of 1981, were allowed by a learned Single Judge by his judgment dated January 11, 1993 on the ground that the penalty of withholding of one increment with cumulative effect is a major penalty and it companyld be imposed only after following the procedure laid down for imposition of a major penalty. Letters Patent Appeals were filed by the appellants against the said judgment of the learned Single Judge in both the cases but the same were dismissed in limine by the Division Bench of the High Court by orders dated April 2, 1993. The appellants have filed these appeals against the said orders of the Division Bench of the High Court. The question which arises for companysideration is whether in the companytext of the Regulations, the penalty of withholding of an increment of pay with cumulative effect is a major penalty. Regulation 4 of the Regulations defines the penalties  minor as well as major  which may be imposed on an officer employee. The provisions relevant for the purpose of the present case are Regulation 4 MINOR PENALTIES Withholding of increments of pay with or without cumulative effect MAJOR PENALTIES Reduction to a lower grade or post, or to a lower stage in a time scale In order to hold that withholding of an increment with cumulative effect is a major penalty, the High Court has placed reliance on the decision of this Court in Kulwant Singh Gill v. State of Punjab, 1991 Supp  1  S.C.C. 504. In that case the Court has companysidered the provisions companytained in Clauses  iv  and  v  of Rule 5 of the Punjab Civil Services  Punishment and Appeals  Rules, 1970, which read as under Rule 5 MINOR PENALTIES Withholding of increments of pay MAJOR PENALTIES reduction to lower stage in a time scale of pay for a specified period, with further directions as to whether or number the government employee will earn increments of pay during the period of such reduction and whether on the expiry of such period, the reduction will or will number have the effect of postponing the future increments of his pay. The Court has held that the penalty of withholding of two increments with cumulative effect falls within Rule 5 v  inasmuch as the effect of such an order by necessary implication is that the employee is reduced in his time scale by two places and it is in perpetuity during the rest of the tenure of his service. While so holding the Court has emphasised that Rule 5 iv  does number empower the disciplinary authority to impose penalty of withholding increments of pay with cumulative effect except after holding inquiry and following the prescribed procedure. Shri Madhava Reddy, the learned senior companynsel for the appellants, has submitted that the scheme of the Regulations differs from that of the Punjab Rules which were under companysideration in Kulwant Singh Gills case  supra  because in Regulation 4 b  of the Regulations it is expressly provided that withholding of increment of pay with cumulative effect is a minor penalty. The submission of Shri Reddy is that in view of such an express provision in the Regulations it is number necessary to companysider whether withholding of an increment with cumulative effect companyld companystitute the major penalty of reduction to a lower grade of post or a lower stage of time scale under Regulation 4 e  of the Regulations.
